An accomplice is a person who helps someone else do something wrong or illegal — not the main person committing the act, but someone who plays a supporting role in it. Think of it this way: if a crime or wrongdoing is a team effort, the accomplice is not the star player, but they are very much part of the team.

For someone to truly be an accomplice, two things must be true at the same time:

1. They must help.
The help can look many different ways — driving someone to the scene of a crime, acting as a lookout, providing a weapon, sharing information, creating a distraction, or even just offering encouragement and a plan. The help doesn't have to be physical. Words, advice, and planning count too.

2. They must know what they are helping with.
This is the most important and most misunderstood part of the word. An accomplice is not someone who was tricked or kept in the dark. They knowingly assisted. If your friend asks you to drive them somewhere and you later find out they robbed a store there — without you knowing beforehand — you are not their accomplice. You were deceived. But if your friend told you exactly what they were going to do and you drove them there anyway, you are their accomplice, even if you never stepped foot inside the store.

Knowledge of the wrongdoing, combined with a choice to help anyway, is what makes someone an accomplice. Remove either one, and the label doesn't apply.

It helps to draw clear lines:

  • An innocent bystander who simply witnesses something wrong is not an accomplice. Watching is not helping.
  • A person who was forced or threatened into helping is generally not considered a true accomplice, because their "help" wasn't a free choice.
  • A person who helped without knowing anything wrong was happening is not an accomplice — they are an unknowing tool, not a willing participant.
  • The main person who actually commits the crime is called the perpetrator or the principal, not the accomplice. The accomplice supports; the perpetrator leads or executes.
The Size of the Role Doesn't Matter

One of the most important things to understand is that an accomplice's role can be enormous or tiny — and they are still an accomplice either way.

Imagine three people plan a theft. One breaks into the building, one stands outside as a lookout, and one simply lent them the tools they needed and stayed home. All three are accomplices to each other (though the law may treat their individual responsibility differently). The person at home who lent the tools played the smallest role, but they knowingly contributed to the crime. That is enough.
The Weight of Being an Accomplice

In the legal world, being an accomplice is serious. The law in most countries holds that a person who knowingly helps commit a crime shares in the guilt of that crime. This means an accomplice can be arrested, charged, and punished — sometimes just as severely as the person who actually "did the deed." The logic is straightforward: without the accomplice's help, the crime may not have happened at all. Their assistance made them morally and legally responsible.

This is why the word carries such a strong negative weight. Calling someone an accomplice is not a neutral description. It is an accusation of deliberate involvement in wrongdoing.

Outside of courts and crime, people use "accomplice" in a looser, sometimes even playful way to describe someone who helped with something mischievous, naughty, or rule-bending — but not necessarily illegal.

For example:

  • "My little brother was my accomplice in sneaking cookies from the kitchen before dinner."
  • "She was my accomplice in convincing the boss to let us leave early on Friday."

In these cases, the word is used with a light or humorous tone. The "wrongdoing" is minor and no one is going to jail. But notice the core idea still holds: someone helped someone else do something they probably shouldn't have, and they did so knowingly.
Rich Examples to Lock It In

Example 1 — Classic crime:
A man plans to rob a jewelry store. His girlfriend knows about the plan. On the day of the robbery, she creates a distraction by pretending to faint outside the store so the security guard rushes out. The man steals the jewels and escapes. She never touched a single piece of jewelry, but she is absolutely his accomplice. She knew the plan and she helped execute it.

Example 2 — No knowledge, no accomplice:
A taxi driver picks up a passenger and drives them to an address. Unknown to the driver, the passenger intends to commit fraud there. The driver is not an accomplice. They had no knowledge of any wrongdoing. They simply did their job.

Example 3 — School cheating:
During an exam, one student whispers answers to their friend. The friend who receives the answers is cheating. The student who whispers them is their accomplice in cheating. Both are guilty, just in different roles.

Example 4 — Planning without showing up:
A hacker helps a criminal gang by writing a piece of software that breaks into a bank's computer system. The hacker never visits the bank, never meets the gang in person, and sits at home the whole time. But they knowingly built the tool that made the crime possible. They are an accomplice.
How It Differs from a Similar Word: "Accessory"

You may sometimes encounter the word accessory used in a similar way, especially in legal contexts. In everyday English, the two words are often used interchangeably. In strict legal language, however, some systems make a distinction: an "accessory after the fact" is someone who helps after the crime is already done — for example, by hiding the criminal, destroying evidence, or lying to the police to protect them. An accomplice, more precisely, helps before or during the crime. But in common everyday use, don't worry too much about this distinction — both words point to someone who is knowingly involved in another person's wrongdoing.
An accomplice is someone who knowingly helps another person do something wrong — sharing in the guilt of that wrongdoing, no matter how big or small their contribution was.
